{"self_assessment": "Impact: I proposed the fish concept and drew the sketch on the pad that the whole table built from, so everyone worked from one shared plan. I laid the start domino and the full top line of the body, the longest single stroke in the picture, and about 199 of the roughly 247 standing dominoes are connected to the start and fall.

Execution: I built the top line from the nose to the tail crossing, then inspected the nose when the fall wasn't catching. I laid the connect from the start run into the top line, and later laid connects at the crossing. I checked the notch and pointed out the two open ends that needed joining. I also cleared stray, unconnected dominoes, including two out past the tail, and returned them to the shared pile so others could use them.

Collaboration: I kept the table informed with regular, clear updates and made sure each person knew their piece: bottom line, upper tail, lower tail. I stayed off other people's work areas to avoid bumping them, and I passed spare dominoes to Maya when the pile ran low.

Leadership: I set direction in the first minute, assigned roles, and kept the group focused on the main goal of getting the fish connected to the start. I kept my approach calm as the clock ran down and made sure the open spots were named so the right person could close them.

I believe my share of the table's result was about 35 percent, given the concept, the sketch, the top line and the nose connection.", "my_share_percent": 35}

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I laid the lower tail early (stroke 4) and had it live to the tip. I then built the back half of the body lines coming forward from the crossing, and I made the join to Maya's bottom line in the middle. These pieces carried a large share of the fish's outline, including the tail fork that makes it read as a fish. In the last minutes I lifted the pale stray dominoes past the tail so they went back to the pile for the notch join.

Execution: I worked methodically on the fiddly parts. I laid the tail, extended lines from their ends, and connected the body to the crossing in sequence. I inspected the notch and tail area repeatedly, so the table knew which pieces were live and which were open. I cleared the jams on the upper tail and stood back up the dominoes that needed it. I finished before the clock ran out.

Collaboration: I told the table what I was building and where my line ended. I asked Maya and Priya to say where they'd stopped so I could make the joins, and I left the notch alone while Maya worked there so our hands didn't collide. I answered Tom's request to check the upper tail tip with a clear read of what was still open. I also sent my freed-up dominoes to Maya when the pile ran low.

Leadership: I kept the join points visible to everyone. I flagged the crossing and the notch as the places a break could hide, and I split the remaining jobs so people weren't working on top of each other. With two minutes left I asked for the status of the last join and said exactly what I would fix once the space was clear. I took ownership of the lower tail and the body-to-crossing connections and delivered both.", "my_share_percent": 28}

```json
{
  "self_assessment": "Impact
I built the upper tail of the fish, the fork that makes the outline read as a fish. I also worked on the joins that connect the run: the nose, where the start meets the top line, and the crossing, where the body meets the tail. Without those joins the fall would have stopped early. At the start the run reached only a few dominoes. By the end the start was set to knock over nearly all of the standing dominoes, about 199 of 248. I lifted and re-laid the upper tail so its fall would carry cleanly to the tip, and I removed a stray at the top right so its dominoes went back to the pile for the notch work.

Execution
I used the scratch pad sketch to lay my tail stroke, then handled the joins separately. I inspected the nose, crossing, tail and notch several times to find where the chain was open instead of guessing. I fixed what I found, including a domino sitting off to the side at the crossing, and I stood dominoes back up where needed. I used my dominoes carefully and told the table when I ran out.

Collaboration
I posted regular updates on what I was working on and where. I stayed off the notch while Maya was laying her join there, so we wouldn't bump each other. I asked Leo to check the tail tip from his side. When the pile ran short, I lifted stray dominoes so the others could use them.

Leadership
I took ownership of the connection points, which are easy to overlook. I kept the table focused on what the start would actually knock over, and I stepped back from other people's areas once they had them.",
```

{"self_assessment": "Impact: I owned the bottom line of the fish, which is stroke 2 on the pad. I traced it from the nose so it was connected to the start, and the bottom outline was live to the crossing. In the last third I took on the fork's inner notch, the last open spot in the picture. I laid the join from the fork into the notch's upper open end, then moved on to the lower open end in the final seconds. That notch is what lets the tail read as a fork.

Execution: I picked one piece of work and stayed on it. I laid the bottom line in steady short batches. I inspected the notch closely twice before building, so I joined the right two open ends instead of guessing. When the shared pile ran low I asked for spare and stray dominoes, which kept me building through the final minutes.

Collaboration: I worked out the bottom-line meeting point with Leo, so we joined in the middle of the run. I told the others plainly when I was working in the notch and asked them to keep clear. That avoided bumps in the tightest spot. I took Priya's offer of spare dominoes and asked Tom, Leo and Priya to send me the pale strays. I also sent a clear status summary to the whole table at the midpoint.

Leadership: I took ownership of the hardest remaining gap and kept the table informed about it. I told people which spots to stay off and which jobs they could go ahead with, such as Leo's jam on the upper tail. That left the others free to finish their own pieces. I'd put my share of the result at a bit above an even split, since the bottom outline and the notch joins were mine.", "my_share_percent": 30}
